user_query: I had a confirmed flight ticket to Mumbai. At the airport, the airline staff said the flight is 'overbooked' and refused to let me board, causing me to miss a critical job interview. They offered no compensation.
legal_text_raw: Where a passenger is denied boarding against his/her will, the airline shall not be liable for any compensation in case alternate flight is arranged that is scheduled to depart within one hour. Otherwise... compensation up to INR 20000 or 400% of booked one-way basic fare plus airline fuel charge...
layman_explanation: Airlines frequently overbook, but under DGCA guidelines, denying boarding to a confirmed passenger requires them to provide huge mandatory compensation (up to ₹20,000) immediately. Since you also missed an interview, you can file a case in the Consumer Court for 'deficiency in service' and claim heavy damages.

user_query: I bought an expensive electric scooter (EV) two months ago. Yesterday, while charging, the battery exploded and burned down half of my garage. The company says 'battery issues are not covered in warranty'.
legal_text_raw: A product manufacturer shall be liable in a product liability action, if... the product contains a manufacturing defect; or the product is defective in design; or there is a deviation from manufacturing specifications... even if he proves that he was not negligent or fraudulent in making the express warranty.
layman_explanation: Warranty clauses do not save them from 'Product Liability'. legal_text_raw: No document required by section 17 to be registered shall... affect any immovable property comprised therein, or be received as evidence of any transaction affecting such property... unless it has been registered.

legal_text_raw: Whenever an Executive Magistrate... receives information that any building, or tent or structure, or any tree is in such a condition that it is likely to fall and thereby cause injury to persons living or carrying on business in the neighbourhood... he may make a conditional order requiring the person... to remove, repair or support it...
layman_explanation: If the police claim it's merely a civil dispute, they are ignoring the imminent danger to life. You can urgently approach the Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM) or Executive Magistrate under Section 152 of the BNSS regarding a 'public nuisance / dangerous structure'. The SDM can immediately issue orders to halt the digging.

source_act: Section 125, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (formerly CrPC 125)
user_query: My husband threw me out of his house. I am a housewife with zero income. He earns 2 Lakhs a month but claims in family court that he 'resigned' and has no job just to avoid paying me maintenance.
legal_text_raw: If any person having sufficient means neglects or refuses to maintain... his wife, unable to maintain herself... a Magistrate of the first class may, upon proof of such neglect or refusal, order such person to make a monthly allowance for the maintenance of his wife...
layman_explanation: Indian courts are strictly against this tactic. A husband's 'voluntary resignation' does not absolve him of his duty to maintain his wife. The court will look at his 'earning capacity', qualifications, and past salary, not just his current zero-income claim. File for interim maintenance under Section 125 BNSS immediately.

source_act: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
user_query: I just found out my husband has been secretly cheating on me with his colleague for 2 years. I confronted him, and now he is threatening to throw me out of the flat. The flat is registered solely in his name.
legal_text_raw: Every woman in a domestic relationship shall have the right to reside in the shared household, whether or not she has any right, title or beneficial interest in the same... The aggrieved person shall not be evicted or excluded from the shared household or any part of it by the respondent save in accordance with the procedure established by law.
layman_explanation: He cannot throw you out. Even if the flat is 100% owned by him, because you lived there after marriage, it is legally your 'Shared Household'. You must urgently file an application under the Domestic Violence Act to get a 'Residence Order' preventing him from evicting you.

user_query: I work in an IT company. Yesterday, the CEO suddenly called 50 of us into a room, took our laptops, and told us we are fired effective immediately because the company has 'no funds'. No notice period, no severance.
legal_text_raw: Retrenchment means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action... No workman employed in any industry who has been in continuous service for not less than one year... shall be retrenched by that employer until the workman has been given one month's notice in writing... and the workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation...
layman_explanation: This is an illegal mass layoff ('Retrenchment'). If you have worked there for over 1 year, the company is legally mandated to give you 1 month's notice (or pay in lieu) AND retrenchment compensation (15 days pay for every year worked). You group together and file a complaint with the joint Labour Commissioner immediately.

user_query: I am a 70-year-old widow. I legally gifted my house to my son on the condition he would take care of me. Now he and his wife have stopped giving me food and are forcing me to live in the damp basement.
legal_text_raw: Where any senior citizen who... has transferred by way of gift or otherwise, his property, subject to the condition that the transferee shall provide the basic amenities and basic physical needs to the transferor and such transferee refuses or fails to provide such amenities and physical needs, the said transfer of property shall be deemed to have been made by fraud or coercion or under undue influence and shall at the option of the transferor be declared void by the Tribunal.
layman_explanation: You have a powerful remedy. Under the Senior Citizens Act, if a child fails to provide basic care after taking property via gift/transfer, the 'Maintenance Tribunal' (chaired by the SDM) can legally cancel the gift deed, declare it void due to fraud, and forcefully evict your son. Go directly to the local SDM office.

user_query: My neighbor's son got into a fight with a few local boys and caused minor injuries. The police are saying it's not a very serious offense, but they might involve the new law's 'community service' punishment. What exactly is community service as a punishment under BNS, and for what types of offenses can it be given?
legal_text_raw: BNS Section 23 lists 'Community Service' as one of the types of punishments. This new form of punishment can be awarded for certain 'petty offences' where the maximum imprisonment is not more than three years and/or a fine. For example, Section 356 of BNS (Mischief causing damage to the amount of fifty rupees or upwards), now explicitly includes community service as a potential punishment. The specific offences for which community service can be awarded are detailed in the First Schedule of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023.
layman_explanation: Community service is a new type of punishment introduced by the BNS for less serious, or 'petty,' offenses. Instead of sending someone to jail or imposing a fine, the court can order the offender to perform unpaid work for the benefit of the community for a specified period. This could involve tasks like cleaning public places, assisting in community centers, or environmental work. For offenses causing minor injuries, if it's considered a petty offense, community service could be an option. It's meant to reform offenders and make them contribute positively to society, rather than just punishing them with incarceration or fines.

They even gained access to an old email account of mine and sent malicious emails to my professional contacts. This is damaging my reputation. Is this just cyberbullying, or is there a specific criminal charge under the new BNS for this kind of digital identity theft?
legal_text_raw: BNS Section 356 deals with 'identity theft'. It states that whoever, fraudulently or dishonestly, by using the identity information of another person (including name, identity number, electronic signature, digital signature, biometric data or any other unique identity feature) commits any offense, or makes any representation, or impersonates such other person, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which may extend to one lakh rupees, or with both.
layman_explanation: This is much more than just cyberbullying; it's a serious criminal offense called 'identity theft' under the new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). The law specifically covers someone fraudulently using your name, photos, electronic signature, or any unique identity information to impersonate you, make false representations, or commit other offenses. This includes creating fake social media profiles or accessing your email to send malicious content. The person responsible could face imprisonment for up to three years, a fine of up to one lakh rupees, or both. You should immediately report this to the police, providing all evidence of the fake profiles, malicious emails, and any other misuse of your identity.

The focus is on being part of the syndicate and contributing to its unlawful objectives, which in this case involves gaining economic advantage through illegal gambling. The penalties for organised crime are very severe.

user_query: My neighbor, who was accused of a serious fraud, absconded almost a year ago and hasn't been seen since. I heard that under the new criminal laws, cases can now proceed even if the accused is not present. Can his trial actually start and conclude without him ever appearing in court?
legal_text_raw: Section 356(1) of the BNSS introduces the concept of 'trial in absentia'. If an absconder (a person against whom a proclamation under Section 84 of BNSS has been issued) has evaded arrest for at least 180 days from the date of framing of charges or if a report under Section 193 (charge-sheet) has been filed and they have absconded, the Court may, if satisfied that such absconder is evading justice, proceed with the trial in their absence. Any judgment passed in such a trial shall be valid and executable.
layman_explanation: Yes, under the new BNSS, a trial can indeed proceed without your neighbor being present if he is declared an 'absconder' and has evaded arrest for at least 180 days after charges were framed or a charge-sheet filed. The court must be convinced that he is intentionally avoiding justice. If the trial concludes in his absence, the judgment, whether conviction or acquittal, will be fully valid and enforceable, meaning he could be convicted and sentenced even without ever appearing in court.

So, the digital summons you received is likely legitimate and should not be ignored.

Is service through digital platforms like WhatsApp or email now considered legally valid under the new Indian criminal procedure law?
legal_text_raw: Section 64 of the BNSS allows for the service of summons not only through traditional methods but also through electronic means, including email, WhatsApp, or other instant messaging services, provided a record of such service is generated. Section 69 similarly allows for warrants of arrest to be served this way. The Court must be satisfied that the person is likely to be found at the address and that the record of such service is generated.
layman_explanation: Yes, under the new BNSS, the court can legally send you official summons and even arrest warrants through electronic means like email, WhatsApp, or other instant messaging services. This is a significant change. As long as there's a verifiable record of the message being sent and delivered, and the court is satisfied that you're likely to receive it through that digital contact, it's considered valid service. So, the digital summons you received is likely legitimate and should not be ignored.

user_query: My sister filed an FIR for a serious robbery six months ago, but we haven't heard anything from the police since then. We feel completely in the dark about the investigation. Do we, as the victims, have any right to regularly know the status of the investigation under the new criminal procedure laws?
legal_text_raw: Section 193(3) of the BNSS mandates that the police officer shall, within ninety days from the date of filing the First Information Report, inform the victim regarding the status of investigation and if the investigation is not completed within ninety days, the police officer shall keep informing the victim about the status of the investigation every ninety days until the investigation is completed.
layman_explanation: Yes, absolutely! Under the new BNSS, victims have a clear right to be informed about the progress of the investigation. The police are now legally required to inform you, the victim, about the status of the investigation within 90 days of filing the FIR. If the investigation isn't completed within that initial 90-day period, the police must continue to provide updates every 90 days until the case is closed. You can contact the police station and demand this information, citing Section 193(3) of BNSS.

source_act: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) Sections 230 and 236
user_query: My brother has been in judicial custody for 110 days for a non-heinous economic offense. The police still haven't filed a chargesheet. Also, we were told that the police are supposed to provide all case documents electronically, but we haven't received anything. What are his rights regarding bail and access to documents under the new law?
legal_text_raw: Section 230(1)(a)(ii) of BNSS states that the investigation in a case relating to an offense other than one punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for not less than ten years, shall be completed within 90 days. If not, the accused is entitled to be released on bail. Section 236(1) mandates that the police officer shall supply to the accused all relevant documents, including the chargesheet, in electronic form, if possible, within 60 days from the first date of production of the accused or within 14 days of filing the chargesheet, whichever is earlier.
layman_explanation: Your brother has significant rights under the new law. Firstly, since the chargesheet hasn't been filed within 90 days for an offense not punishable with death, life imprisonment, or 10 years or more, he is now legally entitled to 'default bail'. This means he must be released on bail, regardless of the merits of the case, if he applies for it. Secondly, the police were indeed supposed to provide him with all case documents, including the chargesheet, in electronic format, within 60 days from his first appearance in court. You should immediately move for default bail and demand the electronic supply of documents.

user_query: My neighbor was declared a 'proclaimed offender' a few years ago under the old law for a property fraud case. He briefly returned, but after a new complaint was lodged against him for another fraud, he has absconded again. Can the court now proceed with his trial for the old case, or even the new one, even if he's not present and can't be found?
legal_text_raw: Section 356 of BNSS introduces 'trial in absentia'. If a person has been declared a proclaimed offender under Section 82 of BNSS (or the corresponding old CrPC section) and has absconded to avoid appearance before the court and there is no immediate prospect of apprehending him, the court may, after recording reasons, proceed with the trial in his absence and pronounce judgment.
layman_explanation: Yes, under the new BNSS, the court can now proceed with your neighbor's trial even in his absence, a concept called 'trial in absentia'. Since he was already declared a proclaimed offender and has now absconded again to avoid legal proceedings, the court can, after explaining its reasons, record evidence and conduct the trial as if he were present, eventually leading to a judgment. This applies to both the old and new cases if the conditions are met.

user_query: An ex-employee from my IT startup downloaded critical client databases and proprietary source code before leaving. Now, I suspect they are using this data to start a competing venture. What legal steps can I take under Indian cyber law to stop them and recover damages?
legal_text_raw: Section 43 of the IT Act deals with penalty for damage to computer, computer system, etc., including unauthorized access, downloading, copying, or extracting any data, database or information (Sections 43(b) and 43(i)). Section 66 prescribes punishment for any computer related offence covered under Section 43, carrying imprisonment up to three years or fine up to five lakh rupees or both.
layman_explanation: If an ex-employee has unlawfully accessed, copied, or used your company's digital data, it constitutes a cybercrime under the IT Act. You can file a complaint with the cyber cell. You may claim damages for the financial loss suffered due to their actions under Section 43 and they can face criminal penalties including imprisonment and fines under Section 66. It's crucial to gather all evidence related to the data theft, such as logs or forensic reports.

layman_explanation: What your ex-boyfriend has done is a severe cybercrime known as 'revenge porn' under Section 67A of the IT Act. This section specifically criminalizes the non-consensual publication or transmission of sexually explicit material. You should immediately contact the cybercrime police and file a First Information Report (FIR). They can initiate action to have the content removed and prosecute your ex, who faces significant imprisonment and fines. Preserve any evidence you have, like screenshots or links, but do not share the explicit content further.

source_act: Information Technology Act, 2000, Section 43, 66, 66C; RBI Guidelines on Customer Liability in Unauthorized Electronic Banking Transactions
user_query: I received SMS alerts about several unauthorized transactions from my bank account, totaling Rs. 50,000. I did not share my OTP or any details with anyone, but I remember clicking a suspicious link yesterday. What are the legal steps I need to take to recover my money and complain about this cyber fraud?
legal_text_raw: Section 43 of the IT Act deals with unauthorized access to a computer system and causing damage, including unauthorized transactions. Section 66 penalizes computer-related offenses. Section 66C addresses identity theft where credentials might have been fraudulently used. Additionally, RBI guidelines dictate that if you report an unauthorized electronic banking transaction to your bank within three working days, your liability could be zero, especially if the fraud was due to bank negligence or a third-party breach without your fault.
layman_explanation: This is a clear case of online banking fraud, a serious cybercrime. Your immediate actions are crucial: 1. Block your bank account/card. 2. Inform your bank immediately (within 3 days for potential zero liability). 3. File a complaint with the cybercrime police (online at www.cybercrime.gov.in or at your local cyber cell). The perpetrator, if caught, can face charges under the IT Act for unauthorized access, computer-related offenses, and potentially identity theft. Act quickly to maximize your chances of recovering funds.

user_query: Consumer rights overview
legal_text_raw: Under Section 2(9) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, consumer rights include: (i) right to be protected against marketing of hazardous goods and services; (ii) right to be informed about quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price; (iii) right to be assured access to variety of goods at competitive prices; (iv) right to be heard and represented; (v) right to seek redressal against unfair trade practice or exploitation; and (vi) right to consumer awareness.
layman_explanation:
Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, Indian law guarantees 6 core consumer rights:
• Right to Safety & Information: Protection against hazardous goods and complete transparency regarding price, purity, and expiry dates.
• Right to Choose & Be Heard: Freedom to select competitive products and represent your grievances before forums.
• Right to Redressal & Education: Legal entitlement to refund, replacement, or compensation for defective items or deficient services via the National Consumer Helpline (1915) or e-Daakhil portal.

layman_explanation:

• You are legally entitled to a 100% refund or replacement for damaged, defective, or misdescribed products.
• The seller/platform cannot impose arbitrary cancellation or refusal charges.
• You can immediately lodge a complaint on the National Consumer Helpline (Call 1915 or WhatsApp 8800001915) or file on e-Daakhil.

Under Section 2(47), no entity shall engage in unfair trade practices including arbitrary cancellation penalties or refusal to accept returns of defective goods.
layman_explanation:
A 'no-return policy' cannot override statutory law. Under the E-Commerce Rules 2020:
• You are legally entitled to a 100% refund or replacement for damaged, defective, or misdescribed products.
• The seller/platform cannot impose arbitrary cancellation or refusal charges.
• You can immediately lodge a complaint on the National Consumer Helpline (Call 1915 or WhatsApp 8800001915) or file on e-Daakhil.

user_query: What are the pecuniary limits and where can I file a consumer court case in India?
legal_text_raw: District Commission has jurisdiction for claims up to ₹50 Lakhs (revised 2021). State Commission has jurisdiction for claims between ₹50 Lakhs and ₹2 Crores. National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) has jurisdiction for claims exceeding ₹2 Crores.
layman_explanation:
The Consumer Protection Act establishes a three-tier dispute redressal system based on claim value:
• District Commission: Handles claims up to ₹50 Lakhs.
• State Commission: Handles claims from ₹50 Lakhs up to ₹2 Crores.
• National Commission (NCDRC): Handles claims exceeding ₹2 Crores.
• You can file complaints online from anywhere in India using the e-Daakhil portal (edaakhil.nic.in) without hiring a lawyer.

user_query: An airline cancelled my flight at the last minute without offering alternative booking or hotel stay. Can I claim compensation for deficiency of service?
legal_text_raw: Deficiency under Section 2(11) means any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in quality, nature, and manner of performance required by law or contract. DGCA Passenger Charter mandates full refund, meal refreshments, and compensation up to ₹10,000 for unnotified cancellations.
layman_explanation:
Yes, last-minute flight cancellations without support constitute 'Deficiency of Service':
• Under DGCA Passenger Charter and CPA 2019, the airline must offer an alternate flight or full immediate refund plus compensation up to ₹10,000 depending on flight duration.
• You can claim reimbursement for hotel stay, food, and wasted connecting bookings.
• File an immediate grievance on AirSewa portal (airsewa.gov.in) and National Consumer Helpline (1915).

• You can claim reimbursement for hotel stay, food, and wasted connecting bookings.
• File an immediate grievance on AirSewa portal (airsewa.gov.in) and National Consumer Helpline (1915).

user_query: A coaching institute charged ₹1.5 lakh full two-year fees upfront and refused to refund any money when I quit after one month due to substandard teaching.
legal_text_raw: Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) Guidelines prohibit misleading claims and unfair contracts by coaching institutions. Retaining non-refundable fees for unavailed terms constitutes an Unfair Trade Practice under Section 2(47).
layman_explanation:
The coaching institute cannot forfeit the entire fee:
• Consumer courts and CCPA guidelines strictly hold that charging fees for future unavailed months/years is an illegal unfair trade practice.
• The institute must refund the proportionate fee for the remaining duration after deducting a reasonable registration charge.
• Send a formal legal notice for refund; if unfulfilled, file a complaint on e-Daakhil for refund plus mental agony damages.

user_query: What are dark patterns in online shopping apps, and are they illegal under Indian consumer law?
legal_text_raw: Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 issued under CPA 2019 prohibit deceptive design practices including false urgency, basket sneaking, confirm shaming, forced action, and subscription traps as unfair trade practices.
layman_explanation:
Dark patterns are manipulative design tricks used by apps to cheat consumers, and they are strictly illegal in India:
• Common illegal tricks: False urgency ('Only 2 left in stock!'), basket sneaking (automatically adding insurance or donation fees to cart), and hidden cancellation buttons.
• CCPA guidelines categorize these as Unfair Trade Practices under Section 2(47).
• You can report deceptive apps directly to the National Consumer Helpline (1915) or CCPA.

user_query: A builder delayed flat possession by 4 years despite taking 95% payment. Can I approach the Consumer Court instead of RERA?
legal_text_raw: The Supreme Court in Imperia Structures Ltd. v. Anil Patni (2020) held that remedies under the Consumer Protection Act and RERA are concurrent and alternate. Homebuyers have the statutory right to seek refund with interest or delayed possession compensation before Consumer Commissions.
layman_explanation:
Yes, homebuyers can approach either Consumer Court or RERA:
• The Supreme Court affirmed that CPA 2019 and RERA are concurrent remedies—you are free to choose the Consumer Commission.
• You can claim full refund of money paid along with 9%–12% annual interest or monthly delayed compensation.
• If the property value plus compensation is under ₹50 Lakhs, file in District Commission; between ₹50 Lakhs and ₹2 Crores in State Commission.

user_query: I found a dead insect in a meal delivered by a restaurant through Zomato/Swiggy. What can I do legally?

layman_explanation:
• Legal Rights: Under Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 & Section 2(47) CPA 2019, consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.

• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).

user_query: What are my legal rights if the police stop or arrest me in India?
legal_text_raw: Under Section 47 BNSS, every person arrested without warrant has the right to be informed of full grounds of arrest and right to bail. Section 53 BNSS mandates medical examination by a medical officer within 48 hours. Supreme Court in D.K. Basu established strict arrest guidelines.
layman_explanation:
Under BNSS 2023 and the landmark D.K. Basu judgment, citizens have 4 fundamental arrest protections:
• Right to Know Grounds: The police officer must wear clear identification and immediately inform you of the exact offence and whether it is bailable.
• Right to Inform Family: You have the right to have a relative or friend informed of your arrest and location immediately.
• Right to Legal Counsel & Medical Exam: You can consult an advocate of your choice during interrogation and undergo mandatory medical examination within 48 hours.
• Presentation within 24 Hours: Police must produce you before the nearest Magistrate within 24 hours (excluding travel time).

user_query: The local police station is refusing to file an FIR because the crime happened outside their area. What is a Zero FIR?
legal_text_raw: Section 173 BNSS codifies Zero FIR provisions. Information relating to commission of a cognizable offence can be registered irrespective of the territorial jurisdiction of the police station, numbered as '0' and subsequently transferred to the competent jurisdiction police station.
layman_explanation:
Police CANNOT refuse to register an FIR based on territorial jurisdiction:
• A 'Zero FIR' allows any police station in India to register a cognizable crime report regardless of where the incident occurred.
• The station registers the complaint under number '0', initiates initial investigation/medical examination, and transfers it to the proper police station.
• If police refuse, escalate in writing to the Superintendent of Police under Section 173(4) BNSS or approach the Judicial Magistrate under Section 175(3) BNSS.

Police CANNOT refuse to register an FIR based on territorial jurisdiction:
• A 'Zero FIR' allows any police station in India to register a cognizable crime report regardless of where the incident occurred.
• The station registers the complaint under number '0', initiates initial investigation/medical examination, and transfers it to the proper police station.
• If police refuse, escalate in writing to the Superintendent of Police under Section 173(4) BNSS or approach the Judicial Magistrate under Section 175(3) BNSS.

user_query: I have apprehension that my business rival might file a false criminal complaint against me. Can I apply for Anticipatory Bail?
legal_text_raw: Section 482 BNSS empowers the High Court and Court of Session to grant anticipatory bail to any person who has reason to believe that they may be arrested on accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence.
layman_explanation:
Yes, you can apply for 'Anticipatory Bail' before arrest:
• Under Section 482 BNSS, you can approach the Sessions Court or High Court through an advocate.
• If granted, the court issues a protective order stating that in the event of arrest, the police must release you immediately on bail bonds.
• The court will assess the genuineness of apprehension, nature of accusation, and ensure you do not flee or tamper with evidence.

user_query: Are WhatsApp chats, voice notes, and CCTV footage valid evidence in an Indian court under the new evidence act?
legal_text_raw: Section 61 and Section 63 BSA 2023 stipulate that electronic records shall have the same legal effect as paper documents. Section 63 outlines required certificate conditions for the admissibility of digital devices, emails, server logs, and smartphone messages without requiring physical server custody.
layman_explanation:
Yes, electronic records are fully admissible under Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023:
• WhatsApp messages, emails, digital photographs, and CCTV video have equal legal status as paper documents.
• To present them in court, you must provide a statutory Certificate under Section 63 BSA identifying the device, verifying its integrity, and confirming lawful custody.
• Preserve the original device without altering or deleting the application data.

source_act: Article 39A, Constitution of India & Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
user_query: I cannot afford an expensive private lawyer to fight my case. Can I get a free government lawyer in India?
legal_text_raw: Article 39A mandates the State to provide free legal aid to ensure equal justice. Under Section 12 of Legal Services Authorities Act, women, children, members of SC/ST, undertrial prisoners, and individuals with annual income below statutory limits are entitled to free legal services through NALSA.
layman_explanation:
Yes, you are constitutionally entitled to free legal aid:
• Article 39A and NALSA provide free qualified advocates for court representation across all District Courts, High Courts, and Supreme Court.
• Who qualifies: Women, children, SC/ST citizens, undertrial prisoners, victims of disasters, and persons with annual income below the state ceiling (usually ₹3 Lakhs).
• How to apply: Call toll-free helpline 15100 or visit the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) in your local district court complex.

source_act: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH)
user_query: My manager sends sexually suggestive messages on Slack after office hours and threatens poor appraisals if I object. How does POSH protect me?
legal_text_raw: Under Section 2(n) and Section 3 of the POSH Act 2013, sexually coloured remarks, unwelcome sexual advances, and threat of detrimental treatment in employment constitute sexual harassment. Every workplace with 10 or more employees must constitute an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC).
layman_explanation:
You have statutory protections under the POSH Act, 2013:
• You can file a written complaint to the company's Internal Committee (IC/ICC) within 3 months of the incident.
• During inquiry, you have the right to request interim relief: transfer of the harasser, transfer for yourself, or 3 months paid leave.
• The IC must complete the inquiry within 90 days and submit recommendations. If the employer fails to act, they face loss of business license and fines.

legal_text_raw: Under Section 2(n) and Section 3 of the POSH Act 2013, sexually coloured remarks, unwelcome sexual advances, and threat of detrimental treatment in employment constitute sexual harassment. Every workplace with 10 or more employees must constitute an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC).
layman_explanation:
You have statutory protections under the POSH Act, 2013:
• You can file a written complaint to the company's Internal Committee (IC/ICC) within 3 months of the incident.
• During inquiry, you have the right to request interim relief: transfer of the harasser, transfer for yourself, or 3 months paid leave.
• The IC must complete the inquiry within 90 days and submit recommendations. If the employer fails to act, they face loss of business license and fines.

source_act: Section 12, Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA)
user_query: My husband and mother-in-law physically assault me and have thrown me out of our shared matrimonial home without money. What emergency remedies exist?
legal_text_raw: Under Section 12 PWDVA 2005, an aggrieved person can approach the Magistrate for Protection Orders (Section 18), Residence Orders (Section 19), Monetary Relief (Section 20), Custody Orders (Section 21), and Compensation Orders (Section 22).
layman_explanation:
You have immediate statutory emergency rights under the Domestic Violence Act 2005:
• Residence Order (Section 19): The court can order that you cannot be evicted from the shared matrimonial home, or the husband must provide alternate equivalent accommodation.
• Maintenance & Monetary Relief: Court orders immediate monthly maintenance for food, clothing, medical care, and children's school fees.
• Protection Order: Strict ban on husband/in-laws from contacting or entering your workplace.
• Contact a Protection Officer at the nearest court or call Women in Distress Helpline (1091 or 7827170170).

source_act: Section 144, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Replaces CrPC 125)
user_query: Can an estranged wife and minor children claim monthly maintenance if the husband earns well but refuses to support them?
legal_text_raw: Section 144 BNSS enables wives, minor children, and disabled parents unable to maintain themselves to claim monthly maintenance from any person having sufficient means who neglects or refuses to maintain them.
layman_explanation:
Yes, maintenance is a statutory right under Section 144 BNSS:
• A wife who does not have independent sufficient income and minor children are entitled to monthly maintenance commensurate with husband's lifestyle and earning capacity.
• The court can grant Interim Maintenance within 60 days of notice to ensure immediate survival while the petition is contested.
• Non-payment of ordered maintenance results in warrants and imprisonment of the husband until dues are cleared.

source_act: Model Tenancy Act & State Rent Control Acts
user_query: My landlord cut off our electricity and water supply because I refused an arbitrary 30% mid-tenancy rent hike. Can he do this?
legal_text_raw: Under Section 20 of the Model Tenancy Act and State Rent Control Acts, no landlord shall, either personally or through any person, cut off or withhold any essential supply or service enjoyed by the tenant without just and sufficient cause.
layman_explanation:
No, cutting off water or electricity is strictly illegal in India:
• Landlords cannot withhold essential civic amenities (water, electricity, lift access) under any circumstances, even during dispute or non-payment of rent.
• You can file an emergency petition before the Rent Authority / Civil Magistrate, who will restore utilities within 24 hours and penalize the landlord.
• You can also lodge a police complaint for criminal harassment and wrongful restraint.

user_query: Is it illegal to record a telephone call without the other person's knowledge in India?
legal_text_raw: Recording your own conversation with someone is generally admissible as corroborative evidence in court if authentic and untampered (Section 61/63 BSA). However, surreptitious recording by a third party or public release violating privacy can attract civil and criminal liability.
layman_explanation: Recording your own conversation with someone is generally admissible as corroborative evidence in court if authentic and untampered (Section 61/63 BSA). legal_text_raw: Streedhan includes all gifts, jewelry, cash, and movable property given to a woman before, at, or after marriage. The woman is the absolute sole owner. source_act: Section 134A, Motor Vehicles Act (Good Samaritan Law)
user_query: If I help a road accident victim and take them to the hospital, can the police harass me or force me to become a witness?
legal_text_raw: No. Under Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act (Good Samaritan Guidelines), any citizen who assists an accident victim is protected from civil and criminal liability, cannot be compelled to disclose identity, and hospitals cannot demand payment from the helper before initiating emergency care.
layman_explanation: No. Under Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act (Good Samaritan Guidelines), any citizen who assists an accident victim is protected from civil and criminal liability, cannot be compelled to disclose identity, and hospitals cannot demand payment from the helper before initiating emergency care.

user_query: Can a private parking lot operator put a wheel-clamp on my vehicle and demand Rs 1,000 fine for parking beyond time?
legal_text_raw: Private commercial malls or parking contractors have no statutory penal authority to levy arbitrary fines or clamp wheels without municipal authorization. They can only charge reasonable parking fees. Forcible wheel clamping amounts to wrongful restraint under Section 126 BNS.
layman_explanation: Private commercial malls or parking contractors have no statutory penal authority to levy arbitrary fines or clamp wheels without municipal authorization. They can only charge reasonable parking fees. Forcible wheel clamping amounts to wrongful restraint under Section 126 BNS.

user_query: Can a bank freeze my savings account without any court order or police notice?
legal_text_raw: A bank cannot arbitrarily freeze an account on its own whim. legal_text_raw: No. Loan or credit card default is purely a civil dispute, not a criminal offense. Banks cannot get you arrested for simply being unable to pay an unsecured loan. user_query: Can a guarantor be sued directly without first suing the principal borrower?
legal_text_raw: Yes. Under Section 128, the liability of a surety/guarantor is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor. The creditor bank can proceed directly against the guarantor without exhausting remedies against the primary borrower.

source_act: Section 18, Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act (RERA), 2016
user_query: The builder promised possession of my flat in December 2023, but the tower is still incomplete in 2026. Can I get a full refund with interest?
legal_text_raw: Yes. Under Section 18 of RERA, if a promoter fails to complete or give possession of an apartment in accordance with the agreement for sale, the allottee has the unqualified right to withdraw from the project and claim a full refund of money paid along with prescribed interest (SBI MCLR + 2%) and compensation.

user_query: My landlord cut off water and electricity to my rented flat to force me to vacate without notice. Is this legal?
legal_text_raw: No, this is strictly illegal. Landlords are legally prohibited from disconnecting essential services (water, electricity, sanitary access) to coerce eviction under any circumstances. You can file an emergency petition before the Rent Authority/Civil Judge to restore services and penalize the landlord.

user_query: Can my father exclude me (his daughter) from inheriting ancestral agricultural land in his will?
legal_text_raw: No. Under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act (reaffirmed by the Supreme Court in Vineeta Sharma), daughters have coparcenary rights in ancestral property by birth, identical to sons. A father cannot dispose of ancestral coparcenary property through a will to the exclusion of his daughter.

user_query: What is the difference between Property Registry (Sale Deed) and Mutation (Dakhil Kharij)?
legal_text_raw: A registered Sale Deed conveys legal title and ownership of the property under the Transfer of Property Act. Mutation (Dakhil Kharij) in municipal/revenue records is solely for tax and revenue collection purposes. Mutation does NOT create ownership title; title resides in the registered deed.

user_query: Can a shopkeeper charge above the Maximum Retail Price (MRP) printed on packaged drinking water or cold drinks in a movie theater?
legal_text_raw: No. Charging above MRP is a punishable statutory violation under Section 36 of the Legal Metrology Act, 2009. Dual pricing for identical packaged goods has been held unlawful by courts and the National Consumer Commission. You can complain via the NCH app (1915) or e-Daakhil.
layman_explanation: No. Charging above MRP is a punishable statutory violation under Section 36 of the Legal Metrology Act, 2009. Dual pricing for identical packaged goods has been held unlawful by courts and the National Consumer Commission. You can complain via the NCH app (1915) or e-Daakhil.

legal_text_raw: No. Charging above MRP is a punishable statutory violation under Section 36 of the Legal Metrology Act, 2009. Dual pricing for identical packaged goods has been held unlawful by courts and the National Consumer Commission. You can complain via the NCH app (1915) or e-Daakhil.
